newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters eye over $15 bln of muni bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters eye over $15 bln of muni bonds.

text.p: U.S. voters Tuesday will decide on about $15.5 billion of municipal bond issues -- the largest slate of bond issues ever -- that would finance everything from roads and bridges to clean water programs, harbor dredging and school buildings, according to a Reuters survey.
An improved voter mood about the economy and the pressure of almost $1 trillion of infrastructure needs could see many of the bond issues approved, according to polls and analysts.
The previous record for bond ballot issues was in 1988 when $15.09 billion of bond issues were on the ballot. Voters at that time approved 92 percent of the issues, or more than $13 billion.
Robert Chamberlin, senior vice president of research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, said the approval rating for bond ballots should be "sky high" this year.
"It's absolutely an ideal setting for passing referenda like we've got," because of strong economies throughout the U.S., he said.

There's a direct corollation between economic conditions and the approval rating, Chamberlin said. The reverse was shown during California's recession in the early 1990s, when only about 40 percent of that state's ballots were approved.
In 1995, 85 percent of the $7 billion of bonds on the national ballot were approved. But in 1994, only 66 percent of the $10 billion of bonds on ballots around the country were approved.
The state referenda also fare better than local and school bonds, because voters do not directly tie their yes votes to higher taxes, according to Chamberlin.
At the local level, however, voters tend to understand better exactly what the pocketbook affect of a "yes" vote will be, so they are more likely to vote them down.
George Leung, a vice president with Moody's Investors Service, a major rating agency, said schools need the most financing.
"It's the greatest area of need," Leung said. "As to whether or not they get approved depends on the area in question."

"I think the mood overall is one in which there is a greater degree of conservatism and efficiency in government that the voters are demanding," he said. "Whether that translates into rejection of bond referendums or other initiatives, really depends on the states or locales in question."
Over 50 percent of the dollar volume of bonds are in three states: California, New York and North Carolina.

California, one of the country's most prolific bond issuers, has the bulk of the bond ballot issues and also the largest single bond ballot issue: a $2 billion Los Angeles Unified School District, Calif., school bond proposal.
North Carolina voters will cast a yea or nay ballot for almost $3 billion of general obligation bonds for schools and highways.

New York State voters will decide on a massive $1.75 billion New York Clean Water, Clean Air Bond Act. If approved, general obligation bond sales would fund a variety of environmental projects throughout the state.
New York Voters appear to be inclined to approve the measure, according to polls.
